# LoopRes: Unlocking the Power of Loops in Pretrained LLMs with Loop Residuals

English · [简体中文](../zh/2611.31094.md) · [Back to the list](../../README.md)

<sub>arXiv 2611.31094 · 2026-11-23 · National University of Singapore</sub>

<img src="../../assets/glyphs/2611.31094.svg" alt="L0-6 (7 layers) -&gt; [L7-20 (14 layers)] x 3 or 7 -&gt; L21-27 (7 layers); injection depth-attention; KV per-pass">

> Finetune a pretrained LLM into a prelude-core-coda loop whose core layers attend over the block outputs of the previous loop, with a trained loop-aware key on each source.

**Category**: Architecture: cross-pass state and residuals · **Status**: draft (numbers not yet re-checked) · **Impact**: cites 1 · stars 88 · HF upvotes 20

[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31094) · [code](https://github.com/NUS-HPC-AI-Lab/LoopRes) · [weights](https://huggingface.co/oahzxl/LoopRes-Qwen3-1.7B)

## Problem

Finetuning pretrained LLMs into loops brings only marginal gains over SFT, which the authors attribute to existing designs compressing the outputs of earlier loops into a narrow pathway. Attention Residuals (AttnRes) let layers read earlier outputs directly, but in a loop the sources are iterates of the same layers that look alike, the AttnRes weights settle early in finetuning, and the growing source set lets layers skip intermediate loops.

## Method

- Split the backbone into a prelude, core and coda of one quarter, one half and one quarter of its layers, cut the core into B=2 blocks, and run the core L=3 (2x compute) or L=7 (4x compute) times.
- Inside the core, apply Block AttnRes. Each sub-layer reads a softmax-weighted sum of the prelude output, earlier block outputs and the current block's partial sum, with its own zero-initialized query in each loop.
- Give each source a trainable loop-aware key, one vector per block per loop initialized from N(0, I), scored by a second query and added to the score of the RMSNorm content key.
- Keep only the block outputs of the latest W=1 loops as sources, so each input has at most (W+1)B+1 sources, and fuse the read into one Triton kernel.

## Loop layout

| Facet | Value |
|---|---|
| Where the loop sits | middle core (prelude-core-coda) |
| Weight sharing | fully tied |
| Passes in training | fixed |
| Passes at test time | fixed |
| Input injection | attention over earlier passes |
| KV cache | per-pass KV |
| Gradient through passes | full BPTT |
| Origin | retrofitted from a pretrained model |
| FFN | dense FFN |
| Attention in the loop | full attention |
| Passes (L7-20) | train 3 or 7; test 3 or 7 |

Shown is Qwen3-1.7B-Base (28 layers). Every backbone is split into a prelude, core and coda of one quarter, one half and one quarter of its layers, and the core is cut into B=2 blocks. Running the core L=3 or L=7 times costs 2x or 4x the backbone's compute, measured in layers passed per token; each loop count is a separately trained model. Inside the core, every sub-layer reads a softmax mix of the prelude output, the block outputs of the previous W=1 loop, the finished blocks of the current loop and the current block's partial sum, instead of the residual stream. The prelude and coda keep the standard residual stream.

## Other findings

- With plain AttnRes in the looped core, the weight on the path through every loop falls from 33.7% with three loops to 0.05% with seven, and the most likely paths never reach the later loops. (Section 2.3; Figure 2e)
- In the learned weights, the first core block mainly updates its own output from the previous loop, and the second block relies most on the first block of the current loop. (Section 3.5; Figure 6a,b)
- Shapley values attribute most of the source selection to the loop-aware key at both compute budgets, with a smaller share for the content key. (Section 3.5; Figure 6c)
- The content key steers simple tokens such as "But" and "Wait" toward shallower outputs, and digits and math symbols toward deeper ones. (Section 3.5; Figure 6d)
- Under AttnRes the content score is almost a fixed preference over sources and barely varies with the token; under LoopRes it varies far more with the token, even as loops deepen. (Section 3.5; Figure 7c,d)
- Scores rise with loop depth and saturate beyond L=5; the authors pick L=3 as the best trade-off between score and compute. (Section 3.3; Figure 5; Table 10)
- On the five harder benchmarks, LoopRes on Qwen3-4B-Base (45.8) scores above SFT on Qwen3-8B-Base (42.9). (Section 3.3; Table 3)

## Comparison

- **Baseline**: SFT (the same backbone finetuned without looping) and 8 looped designs reimplemented on the same backbone and finetuned on the same data with the same hyperparameters. Ouro, TaH2-fixed, CloseLoop, InfiLoop and BRT loop all layers (L=2 and 4); Huginn, Hyperloop and WMRE loop the middle half, as LoopRes does (L=3 and 7).
- **Held fixed**: N (unique parameters), D (training tokens)
- **Differs**: F (training FLOPs), L (executed layers per token), KV (KV cache per token)
- **Baseline hyperparameters**: shared with the looped model
- **Headline claim**: On Qwen3-1.7B-Base at 2x compute, LoopRes raises the average of seven math and code scores from 43.2 (SFT) to 55.8, a 29.1% gain, against 49.2 (13.9%) for the strongest baseline, BRT. At 4x compute it reaches 57.8 (33.7%), against 51.8 (19.8%) for Huginn. (Abstract; Table 1)

## Caveats

- Finetuning only. The 1.7B runs use 572K math and code conversations (3.1B tokens) for 12,000 steps on 16,384-token sequences, evaluation covers math and code benchmarks only, and the authors say broader tasks and RL remain untested.
- Compute is not matched against SFT; LoopRes passes 2x or 4x the backbone's layers per token, and the looped baselines are compared at the same 2x and 4x. LoopRes adds per-loop query and key vectors, and the paper prints no parameter counts.
- The paper reports no KV cache sizes; the official code caches keys and values for every (layer, loop step) pass.
- No run applies AttnRes or LoopRes without looping. The closest control for the residual change is Huginn with and without AttnRes on the same looped core (Tables 1 and 5).
- All models share one hyperparameter set (learning rate 3e-5, picked from a five-value sweep, Appendix A.4); the baselines are not tuned separately.
- Baselines are reimplemented as finetunes of the same backbone with changes, such as Ouro without its exit gate, Huginn with a fixed loop count and Parcae's diagonal injection, InfiLoop with a single running average and BRT with seven blocks of four layers; six of the originals pretrain from scratch (Appendix A.2).
- Every token runs all L loops in training and at inference.

## Open questions stated by the authors

- Can combining LoopRes with reinforcement learning cut the rollout budget, given its lower cost of matching SFT on long outputs?
- Can the model decide how many loops each token or sequence needs?
- The loop-depth scaling curve has not saturated on larger backbones; how does looping behave at greater scale?
- The learned loop dependencies follow clear patterns; could a simpler, fixed connection scheme capture most of the benefit without learned attention weights?
